name: Spongeware
region: Glasgow, Staffordshire and Ohio, Britain and the United States
summary: Cheap white earthenware that potters dabbed with a cut sea sponge dipped in colour. The soft blue or green mottle fills a bowl, a jug or a canister with little skill.

philosophy.core_thesis: A sponge turns a cheap white pot into a coloured one in a few seconds, so that a worker without training can decorate a hundred pieces in an hour.
design_principles: Make a plain, white-bodied pot in a mould or on a jigger, with a wall 4 to 6 mm thick.
Dab the colour on the biscuit with a cut sponge dipped in a stain; use 1 to 4 colours.
Stamp the sponge in a pattern of dots, or dab it in a loose mottle.
Keep a plain white band at the rim and the foot for contrast.
Use blue first, then green, brown and red; add a hand-painted line or a flower in some pieces.
Dip the pot in clear glaze and fire it at about 1050 to 1100 °C.
Make useful shapes: a mixing bowl, a jug, a butter dish and a canister.
anti_patterns: A deep, glossy glaze with pooling
A unified white ground with no colour

form.shape: Mixing bowls, pitchers, butter dishes, canisters, chamber pots and plates; the forms are plain and stack well.
form.profile: A deep bowl with a flared wall and a flat foot; a jug with a round belly and a strap handle.
form.foot_and_rim: A flat foot or a thin turned foot ring left clear of the sponge; a plain rolled rim or a ring of white.
form.proportion: A mixing bowl is 18 to 28 cm wide; wall 4 to 6 mm; a jug 15 to 20 cm high.
rules: Keep a clear band at the rim for the sponge to end on.
Use plain, moulded shapes that a worker can decorate fast.
Glaze the outside and the inside.

bodies.rule: Use a white or cream earthenware so that the sponge colour shows. American work also uses a pale stoneware. Keep red clay out: it dulls the colour.

methods: sponging the biscuit with a cut sponge
hand-painting a line at the rim
forming.joins: Handles are cast or pressed and fixed with slip; moulded ribs run on the outside of some bowls.
forming.details: The soft edge of a sponge print, small gaps between the dabs, and a clear white band at the rim.

glaze.pattern: A loose mottle of blue, green or brown dabs in a ring round the body; some pieces add a painted flower, a bird or a band.
glaze.gloss: A clear gloss of about 60 to 85 GU; the sponge colour sits under it.
glaze.wear: The glaze crazes with age in a fine net; the colour stays under it.

palette.strategy: Blue, green and brown dabs on white; a red or yellow accent in the more costly pieces.

firing.kiln: A coal-fired bottle or round kiln; biscuit firing, sponging and a clear glaze firing.
processes: dabbing the colour with a sponge
firing.scale: A worker sponged a hundred or more pieces in an hour; Scottish firms shipped spongeware to North America by the crate.
firing.signs: Soft-edged dabs, a clear band at the rim, and a fine crazing net in the glaze.

pieces.form: Large mixing bowl with a blue sponge ring and a white rim
Jug with a green and brown sponged body and a strap handle
Butter dish with a sponged lid and a hand-painted band
Canister with a blue and red sponged wall

positive: soft blue sponge dabs on white
clear white band at the rim
still-life museum photograph, soft north light

emotion.target_response: A soft, friendly lightness: the viewer sees a blue mottle on a white bowl and thinks of a cottage kitchen.

a mixing bowl brief with a loose blue dab pattern
avoid_when: the brief needs a precise printed pattern
the brief needs stoneware salt glaze
the brief wants thin white porcelain

modifiers.how: Replace the dabs with turned bands in slip on a pale body.

modifiers.request: blue and white bands, twentieth century
modifiers.how: Replace the dabs with four hand-banded stripes in blue on white.
